speaker: Maya (Facilitator)
text: Welcome everyone. Today we're EventStorming Acme's order management flow. Let's start with the big picture — call out domain events, things that happen, in past tense. Don't worry about order yet.

speaker: Sam (Product)
text: The first thing that matters to the business is when a customer places an order. So: Order Placed.

speaker: Anya (Dev)
text: Before that the customer adds items to a cart and checks out. Cart Checked Out happens, then Order Placed.

speaker: Ben (Dev)
text: Once the order is placed we need to take their money. Payment Authorized, then later Payment Captured.

speaker: Raj (Finance)
text: Right, authorization and capture are different events for us. We authorize at checkout but only capture when the goods actually ship.

speaker: Lena (Operations)
text: From the warehouse side the important events are Inventory Reserved, then Shipment Created, Order Picked, Order Packed, and Order Shipped.

speaker: Sam (Product)
text: And eventually Order Delivered. Customers care a lot about that one.

speaker: Maya (Facilitator)
text: Great, lots of events. Let's also capture the unhappy paths.

speaker: Ben (Dev)
text: Payment Declined is a big one. Also Order Cancelled and Refund Issued.

speaker: Lena (Operations)
text: Out Of Stock Detected too — sometimes we can't fulfill even after the order is placed.

speaker: Maya (Facilitator)
text: Now let's add the commands that cause these events, and who issues them — the actors.

speaker: Anya (Dev)
text: The Customer issues Place Order, which produces Order Placed. The Customer is the actor there.

speaker: Ben (Dev)
text: Place Order triggers a Authorize Payment command against the payment gateway. That's Stripe for us.

speaker: Raj (Finance)
text: The payment gateway is an external system. We don't own it, we just call it and react to webhooks.

speaker: Lena (Operations)
text: A Warehouse Operator issues Pick Order and Pack Order. The carrier — also external — gives us tracking when we Create Shipment.

speaker: Maya (Facilitator)
text: Let's talk policies. A policy is a 'whenever X happened, then do Y' reaction. What reacts to Order Placed?

speaker: Sam (Product)
text: Whenever an order is placed, we should reserve the inventory immediately so we don't oversell. So Order Placed leads to Reserve Inventory.

speaker: Lena (Operations)
text: Hmm, that's not how it works in the warehouse today. We only reserve inventory after the payment is captured. Reserving on Order Placed would hold stock for orders that never pay.

speaker: Sam (Product)
text: But if we wait for capture, two customers can buy the last unit during checkout and we oversell. Marketing has complained about this exact thing.

speaker: Lena (Operations)
text: And finance has complained about stock being held hostage by abandoned orders. We genuinely do it after capture right now.

speaker: Maya (Facilitator)
text: Good — let's mark that as a hotspot. There's a real disagreement about when inventory gets reserved: at Order Placed versus after Payment Captured. We'll flag it rather than resolve it now.

speaker: Anya (Dev)
text: There's also ambiguity in what 'Order Confirmed' even means. To me an order is confirmed once payment is authorized.

speaker: Raj (Finance)
text: I'd say an order isn't really confirmed until payment is captured and we've committed to ship. Those are very different points in time.

speaker: Maya (Facilitator)
text: Another hotspot then — 'confirmed' is vague and means different things to different people. Let's surface that.

speaker: Ben (Dev)
text: Whenever Payment Captured happens, a policy notifies the customer. Notification Sent is the event.

speaker: Sam (Product)
text: We also email them on Order Shipped and Order Delivered. The notifications feel like their own concern, honestly.

speaker: Maya (Facilitator)
text: Let's start grouping these into bounded contexts — clusters of language and responsibility that hang together.

speaker: Anya (Dev)
text: I see an Ordering context: cart, checkout, Place Order, Order Placed, Order Cancelled. The ubiquitous language there is Order, Line Item, Cart.

speaker: Raj (Finance)
text: Payments is clearly its own context: Authorize, Capture, Refund, talking to the gateway. Language is Authorization, Capture, Settlement.

speaker: Lena (Operations)
text: Fulfillment is its own world: Pick, Pack, Create Shipment, Order Shipped, carrier integration. We say Shipment, Pick List, Package.

speaker: Sam (Product)
text: Inventory feels separate again — Reserve, Release, Out Of Stock. Stock levels, reservations, warehouses.

speaker: Ben (Dev)
text: And Notifications — emails and SMS reacting to events from everywhere. Probably a supporting context.

speaker: Maya (Facilitator)
text: Which of these are core domain versus supporting versus generic?

speaker: Sam (Product)
text: Ordering is core — that's where our competitive logic lives, promotions, bundling, all that.

speaker: Raj (Finance)
text: Payments is mostly generic — we lean on Stripe. We shouldn't be reinventing settlement.

speaker: Lena (Operations)
text: Fulfillment is core-ish for us actually, our routing and SLA logic is a differentiator.

speaker: Ben (Dev)
text: Notifications is supporting, and arguably we could buy it.

speaker: Maya (Facilitator)
text: How do these contexts talk to each other? Let's capture the messages between them.

speaker: Anya (Dev)
text: Ordering publishes Order Placed. Payments subscribes to it to start authorization.

speaker: Raj (Finance)
text: Payments publishes Payment Captured. Fulfillment and Inventory both care about that.

speaker: Lena (Operations)
text: Fulfillment publishes Order Shipped, which Ordering needs to update order status, and Notifications needs to email the customer.

speaker: Sam (Product)
text: Inventory publishes Out Of Stock Detected — Ordering has to react by cancelling or backordering.

speaker: Maya (Facilitator)
text: What read models do actors need to make decisions? Information someone looks at before issuing a command.

speaker: Lena (Operations)
text: The Warehouse Operator needs a Pick List read model — what to pick and where it is in the warehouse.

speaker: Sam (Product)
text: The Customer needs an Order Status view, and a Product Availability view before they even buy.

speaker: Raj (Finance)
text: Finance needs a Settlement Report read model reconciling captures against shipments.

speaker: Anya (Dev)
text: One assumption we're making: there's a single warehouse. The whole reservation model gets harder with multiple fulfillment centers.

speaker: Ben (Dev)
text: We're also assuming every customer is pre-registered with a saved payment method. Guest checkout would change Ordering and Payments quite a bit.

speaker: Maya (Facilitator)
text: Good assumptions to record. Anything still unclear or risky we haven't named?

speaker: Raj (Finance)
text: Refund flow is hand-wavy. Who initiates a refund and what happens to a reservation that was never shipped is undefined.

speaker: Lena (Operations)
text: And partial shipments — if half the order is in stock, can we ship part now? We've never decided. That'll bite us.

speaker: Sam (Product)
text: Cancellation after capture but before shipping is also fuzzy. Is that a refund, a void, what?

speaker: Maya (Facilitator)
text: Before we wrap, let's walk two concrete orders end to end. That usually exposes rules hiding behind our nouns.

speaker: Sam (Product)
text: Use a normal in-stock order first: one customer, two items, standard delivery, saved card.

speaker: Anya (Dev)
text: The customer checks the cart totals, chooses delivery, and submits Place Order. We should call out Price Confirmed before Order Placed because promotions can expire.

speaker: Sam (Product)
text: Agreed. If the price changed, the customer must accept it. We must not silently place an order at a different total.

speaker: Maya (Facilitator)
text: So Price Changed is a rejection outcome and Confirm Price Change is a customer command. What happens next on the normal path?

speaker: Ben (Dev)
text: Order Placed triggers Authorize Payment. Stripe returns Payment Authorized, and only then can the order progress.

speaker: Lena (Operations)
text: The warehouse needs a Release To Warehouse command. We don't want unreviewed or risky orders appearing on the pick list.

speaker: Raj (Finance)
text: What makes an order risky? We have a fraud score from Stripe Radar, but Finance manually reviews anything above our threshold.

speaker: Maya (Facilitator)
text: Let's add Fraud Review Requested, a Finance Analyst actor, Approve Order and Reject Order commands, and the events Order Approved and Order Rejected.

speaker: Sam (Product)
text: That also means the customer status should say Under Review rather than pretending the order is confirmed.

speaker: Anya (Dev)
text: Once approved, Release To Warehouse produces Order Released. Fulfillment can then decide which warehouse should handle it.

speaker: Lena (Operations)
text: For today's single-warehouse scope that decision is trivial, but let's keep Warehouse Assigned as an event so the future boundary is visible.

speaker: Maya (Facilitator)
text: Now take the last-unit scenario. Two customers check out within seconds. Where must the invariant live?

speaker: Lena (Operations)
text: Inventory must guarantee that available quantity never goes below zero. A reservation needs a quantity, warehouse, order id, and expiry time.

speaker: Ben (Dev)
text: Reserve Inventory should either emit Inventory Reserved or Inventory Reservation Rejected. We need an idempotency key because messages can be delivered twice.

speaker: Sam (Product)
text: If reservation is rejected, Ordering should not immediately cancel. The customer may accept a backorder if we show an expected date.

speaker: Maya (Facilitator)
text: That introduces Offer Backorder, Backorder Accepted, and Backorder Declined. Who calculates the expected availability date?

speaker: Lena (Operations)
text: Inventory Planning owns replenishment dates. Fulfillment consumes an Availability Projection read model but should not calculate supply.

speaker: Anya (Dev)
text: That sounds like another bounded context: Inventory Planning owns stock projections, while Fulfillment owns the physical shipment lifecycle.

speaker: Maya (Facilitator)
text: Good boundary signal. Let's mark it as a candidate rather than force a split today.

speaker: Raj (Finance)
text: On reservation expiry, we should release the authorization too. Stripe authorizations do not last forever and can expire independently.

speaker: Ben (Dev)
text: We need Authorization Expiring Soon and Authorization Expired from Stripe, plus Reauthorize Payment if fulfillment is delayed.

speaker: Sam (Product)
text: The customer must be notified before reauthorization if the amount or delivery promise changed.

speaker: Maya (Facilitator)
text: Let's test cancellation. A customer cancels before picking. What business facts occur?

speaker: Lena (Operations)
text: Cancellation Requested arrives in Fulfillment. If picking has not started, we accept it, emit Fulfillment Cancelled, and release inventory.

speaker: Lena (Operations)
text: If picking already started, a supervisor decides whether to stop the work. After carrier handoff, cancellation becomes a return instead.

speaker: Sam (Product)
text: Ordering needs Cancellation Accepted or Cancellation Rejected so the customer sees a truthful result, not just a submitted request.

speaker: Raj (Finance)
text: Before capture we void the authorization. After capture we issue a refund. Those are distinct commands and financial events.

speaker: Anya (Dev)
text: So Order Cancelled cannot itself tell Payment what to do without knowing whether capture happened. Payment should decide from its own state.

speaker: Maya (Facilitator)
text: Exactly. Ordering publishes Order Cancelled; Payment translates that into Void Authorization or Issue Refund based on its lifecycle.

speaker: Ben (Dev)
text: We also need duplicate webhook handling. Payment Captured can arrive twice, and a retry must not charge the customer again.

speaker: Raj (Finance)
text: The invariant is one successful capture per payment attempt, with every gateway event retained for reconciliation.

speaker: Maya (Facilitator)
text: What operational views are essential before this model can guide implementation?

speaker: Lena (Operations)
text: An Exceptions Queue showing stuck reservations, failed labels, overdue picks, and shipments without carrier updates.

speaker: Raj (Finance)
text: A Payment Exceptions view showing declines, expired authorizations, capture mismatches, and refunds awaiting settlement.

speaker: Sam (Product)
text: Customer Support needs a single Order Timeline assembled from all contexts, but each context remains authoritative for its own facts.

speaker: Maya (Facilitator)
text: Excellent. We now have a thirty-minute sample with a happy path, scarce-resource conflict, fraud review, backorders, cancellation, payment recovery, and concrete read models. Let's wrap here.

speaker: Maya (Facilitator)
text: Final check: keep the inventory timing and Order Confirmed language as open hotspots, record the candidate Inventory Planning boundary, and schedule owners for the unresolved decisions.
